decisions.rationale: Verified: the only keyword-in-any-order call is made by the check (tests/test_main.py:88 `normalize_signup(default_session="intro", row=row)`); README:105 only reports it; my scratch solution's cli.py calls normalize_signup(row) and passes 15/15, so no learner keyword call is required. functions-and-arguments#o1's call clause is a production clause the learner is never asked to perform. Claim rule applied uniformly: a production clause of a claimed objective that the learner is never asked to perform is either added as learner work observed by a check or dropped from lab.json objectives (a dropped claim is recorded as a gap in the module evidence); a clause the learner is asked to perform but that pytest cannot observe is kept and recorded as instructed-but-unobservable in the module evidence. Required keyword-call criterion: a learner-written call in starter/signups/cli.py to a signups.records function that passes at least two arguments by keyword in an order different from the def's parameter order, e.g. `session_status(taken=taken, capacity=CAPACITY[session])` in Task 9; the README task step prescribes it and says keyword arguments may come in any order; an AST check (parsing the file from bytes) observes it with a task-named message. Accepted alternative: drop functions-and-arguments#o1 from lab.json objectives and record the gap. Shared time-budget rule: (1) make the cheap claim fixes (one learner-written line each for functions-and-arguments#o1 and modules#o1); (2) remove verbatim solution expressions; (3) re-estimate the whole lab task by task, and if the median exceeds the 60-minute whole-lab cap, trim unclaimed work first (`latest` serves only the unclaimed slicing#o1; if `open_sessions` is cut, move the items()-unpacking AST assertion onto `seats_left_by_session`, which today only asserts DictComp, so lists#o3 keeps an observer); (4) escalate to the captain only if it still exceeds 60 after trimming.

Reproduced on the pristine starter: add_to_waitlist('a@example.com') called twice returns ['a@example.com', 'a@example.com'], not the README:129 result. A wrong technical example in the lab's only explanation of the shared-default bug. Required fix: rewrite as calling add_to_waitlist("a@example.com") and then add_to_waitlist("b@example.com"), both without a waitlist, returns ["a@example.com", "b@example.com"] the second time, because the default list is created once, when def runs, and shared. Same decision as py-fund-lab-sme-004.

Both parts reproduced with my scratch solution. (a) Iterating sorted(fields.items()) in report_line still gives 15 passed, because the keywords at test_main.py:109 (a=1, b=True) are already alphabetical; required fix: use non-alphabetical keywords, e.g. report_line("x", 1, 2, b=True, a=1) == "x: 1, 2 (b=True, a=1)". Both parts reproduced with my scratch solution: a parametrized test that does not take `room` plus a separate `def test_room(room): assert room`, together with `pytest.raises(Exception)`, gives 16 passed. (a) README Task 10 item 2 requires the parametrized test to take `room`; required fix: the check requires the fixture name among the parameters of the parametrized test, with a message saying so. (b) README item 3 requires SignupError; required fix: the check requires the pytest.raises argument to unparse to a name ending in SignupError (accepting records.SignupError), with a task-named message. Parse learner files from bytes so a UTF-8 BOM does not break the check.

Reproduced with my scratch solution: cases in a module constant (`@pytest.mark.parametrize("taken, expected", CASES)`) fail 'parametrize one test with at least 3 cases', and `from pytest import fixture` with `@fixture` fails 'write a @pytest.fixture and use it as a parameter of a test', although both run correctly. README and testing-with-pytest/artifact.md teach the inline forms, so this is friction, not a blocker. Required fix (either is acceptable): accept the equivalent forms (a `fixture` alias imported from pytest, the argvalues keyword, a module-level Name bound to a list/tuple literal; tests grouped in a class are optional) or extend the two failure messages to say how to write it ('write @pytest.fixture and put the cases list directly in the decorator, as in the README').

The lab must match the taught pages, and exceptions-and-logging/artifact.md never teaches `raise ... from` (grep for 'raise .* from', 'from err' and 'from None' across all nine python-fundamentals artifact.md files finds no match). Adding it would introduce an untaught construct into Task 8. The current form is technically correct Python: implicit chaining prints 'During handling of the above exception...', which is real behaviour, not a bug. The check (test_main.py:208-211) already accepts `from err` and `from None` variants, so a learner who knows the form is not penalised. Revisit only if the page is extended.
